attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, sprite code, score and countdown, on A button press, on countdown end.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you name the player sprite using camelCase and select an image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What sprite image might you use as the player? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that camelCase replaces spaces in text with capital letters.
steps.instructions:
Add a player sprite and a food or collectible sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under // sprite code. Click the palette to select a sprite, then replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase that describes what it is, such as playerSprite


Click ▶ to see the player sprite appear in the center of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite in controller.moveSprite(sprite)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which values might you use as x and y coordinates, so that the player sprite appears on the left side of the screen?

❓ What might you change the vx and vy parameters to in the moveSprite code, so that the player sprite moves at a reasonable speed around the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the moveSprite code has optional vx and vy parameters. They can use number arguments to set the player’s speed in a given direction, separating each parameter with a comma ,.
steps.instructions:
Set the player sprite’s position and on screen movement!


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] under the code that created the player sprite. Update the sprite’s name and the x (0-160) and y (0-120) parameters so that the sprite appears on the left side of the screen. 


Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the line of code that sets the player sprite’s position. Inside the parentheses, replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the line of code that moves the player sprite with buttons. Update the player sprite’s name, and use the default argument true so the sprite will stay in screen.


Click ▶ to move the player sprite around and notice how it stays in screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the x and y parameters inside the parentheses of setPosition so that  randint is used to select a coordinate from a range of values?
steps.instructions:
Add a food sprite and set its starting location to a random position on screen.


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under // sprite code. Click the palette to select a sprite, then replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase that describes what it is, such as foodSprite.


Open Sprites and drag out [set (mySprite) position to x y] under the code that creates the food sprite. Update the sprite’s name, then type randint(0, screen.width) for the x parameter and randint(0, screen.height) for the y parameter to place the sprite randomly on screen.


Click ▶ to see the food sprite appear in a random position.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you put the  if/else conditional inside the curly brackets of the controller.A event?
steps.instructions:
Add a button press event that checks if the player sprite is overlapping the food sprite.


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath the // on A button press comment.


Open Logic and drag [if/else] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

if (true) {...} else {...}

The if/else conditional acts as a block statement nested inside the curly brackets of the controller.A event. It is indented and contains its own set of curly brackets { } to place code inside of.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update both sprites’ names in mySprite.overlapsWith(other)?
steps.instructions:
Change the food sprite’s position when the player sprite catches it!


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition then open Sprites and drag [(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)] inside the parentheses. Replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite and otherSprite with the name of the food sprite.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the code that sets the food sprite’s position under // sprite code. Click inside the curly brackets of the if condition and paste (Ctrl + V) the code.


Click ▶ and move the player sprite on top of the food sprite. Press the A button to see the food sprite move to a new random position.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the argument inside info.changeScoreBy() so that the score increases if the player overlaps with the food sprite, but decreases if it’s not overlapping with the food sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed and the player sprite is overlapping the food sprite? What happens when the A button is pressed and the player sprite is not overlapping the food sprite?

❓ Which keys do you press at the same time to copy code? Which keys do you press at the same time to paste code?

❓ When will the else condition’s code run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain the added logic of the conditional to the ninja: Whenever the A button is pressed, if the player sprite is overlapping the food sprite, then the food sprite will be repositioned, a point will be added, and a sound will play. If the A button is pressed and the player sprite is not overlapping the food sprite, a point will be lost and a different sound will play.

💡 Remind the ninja that the code in the else condition’s block statement will only run if the the if condition is false.

💡 Help the ninja practice highlighting the score and music code to copy and paste it below. Remind the ninja that the code should be placed inside the else condition’s curly brackets.
steps.instructions:
Change the score when the A button is pressed, depending on whether the player sprite is overlapping the foodsprite.


Open Info, and drag out [set score to (value)] under // score and countdown Leave the default argument set to 0. 


Open Info and drag [change score by (1)] inside the curly brackets of the if condition inside the controller.A event, below the position code. Use the default argument 1.


Add a sound effect by opening Music and dragging [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] below the code that changes the score. Change the sound by deleting .baDing then typing . after music to open the code completion tool of possible sounds. Select one that fits the theme of scoring a point.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the score and music code, then paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets of the else condition’s block statement. Update the changeScoreBy argument to a negative value and select a new sound that fits the theme of losing a point.


Click ▶ and press the A button when the sprites overlap and when the sprites do not overlap to see and hear what happens!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add onCountdownEnd to the editor, then drag an if/else conditional inside?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How long should the countdown last in this project?

❓ What condition might be checked when the timer ends?

❓ Why should the conditional be placed inside the curly brackets of the onCountdownEnd function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja understand how the if/else conditional is nested inside of the onCountdownEnd function and that it has its own set of curly brackets. 

💡 Remind the ninja that code inside of curly brackets { } is called a block statement. This code is indented to make it easier for coders to read.
steps.instructions:
Add a countdown timer to your project! 


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] below the code that sets the score under // score and countdown. Leave the default argument set to 10 or update it to a different number of seconds.


Open Info and drag [run code on countdown end] under // on countdown end. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

info.onCountdownEnd(function() {... }

Open Logic and drag [if/else] inside the curly brackets { } of onCountdownEnd. The if/else conditional acts as a block statement nested inside the curly brackets of the onCountdownEnd function. It is indented and contains its own set of curly brackets { } to place code inside of. This code will check if a certain condition is true when the countdown reaches 0.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check the syntax to make sure each pair of parentheses and curly brackets has an opening and closing set?
steps.instructions:
Code the game to end in a win or loss, depending on how many points the player sprite has when the countdown ends!


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition. Open Info and drag [score] into the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


info.score() 


Type > 4 after the score code inside the parentheses, so that the condition reads: (info.score() > 4). If the score is greater than 4 when the timer runs out, the code inside the if condition will run.


Open Game and drag [use effect (effects.confetti) for (true)] and [game over (true)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition. Leave the win parameter set to true in both functions.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the gameOver and setGameOverEffect functions and paste (Ctrl + V) them inside the curly brackets { } of the else condition. Change the win parameter to false in both functions, and update the effect parameter in the setGameOverEffect function.


Click ▶ to see different game over screens appear, depending on the score when the timer runs out!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1-15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!


Open Scene, then drag [set background color to (color)] under // set up. Inside the parentheses, replace 0 with a number between 1-15 to set the background color. 


Open Game, drag out [show long text (str) (layout)] under the code that sets the background color. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to see the background color and dialog box appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how do the nested block statements inside the curly brackets appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Going Bananas!
subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses conditionals and nested block statements to have the user collect items and increase their score.

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name, set its position, move it with the controller, and keep it in the screen.
Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position to a random value.
Use a button press event that runs code when the A button is pressed. Place a conditional statement inside the event.
Use the overlapsWith function to move a sprite inside the if conditional statement.
Use an if conditional statement that checks to see if the player has scored more than 4 points.
Use game over functions with matching effects when the player wins or loses.
Change the background color, add sound effects, and use long text to provide directions for the user.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about conditionals and nested block statements. Nested block statements are created when code inside of curly brackets is placed inside of another chunk of code in curly brackets, such as placing a conditional inside of a forever loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Curly Brackets All the Way Down
badges.description: Use nested block statements to place one block statement inside another in JavaScript.

badges.title: If at First You Don’t Succeed
badges.description: Use  “if” and “if / else” statements in JavaScript.

badges.title: ...or Else
badges.description: Use an “else if” statement in JavaScript.

badges.title: Until the End of Time
badges.description: Use a forever loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: Hey I’m Walking Here
badges.description: Use the overlapsWith function to see if two sprites are overlapping.

badges.title: Gaming the System
badges.description: Use the setGameOverEffect and gameOver functions to customize game over screens.

badges.title: The Final Countdown
badges.description: Use the info.onCountdownEnd function to run code when the countdown reaches zero.

badges.title: Playing the Odds
badges.description: Use the Math.percentChance function inside an if statement to add randomness to a project.

badges.title: A Flair for the Dramatic
badges.description: Add a custom sprite effect to a sprite.

badges.title: Let’s Try That Again
badges.description: Use the game.reset function to restart a project.
